title: Gifts for Silver Collectors: 11 Ideas a Stacker Will Use
summary: Gifts for silver collectors who stack: proof and bullion Silver Eagles, 10 oz bars, pre-1965 dimes, and the scale, tubes and loupe they use on every coin.
body_markdown:
A silver collector wants one of two things from a gift. Either more silver in a format they already buy, which might be a 1 oz Silver Eagle, a 10 oz bar or a few dollars face of pre-1965 dimes, or the gear they reach for every time a new coin arrives, like a scale that reads to 0.01 g, tubes that fit their coins and a decent loupe. Every item below comes with its weight, fineness and issuer, since a stacker is going to check those anyway. Full disclosure: Pure is our marketplace for coins and bullion, and the metal links here go there. If the person you are shopping for cares more about history than ounces, our[gifts for coin collectors](https://www.collectpure.com/blog/gifts-for-coin-collectors) list will serve you better.


Before buying anything, try to find out what is already in their tubes without tipping them off. Silver Eagles, Britannias, generic rounds and bars each fit different holders, and a stacker who has settled on one kind usually wants more of the same.


## 1. A proof Silver Eagle from a year that means something


Proofs are the collector version of the American Silver Eagle: mirror fields, frosted design, and a[presentation case with a certificate of authenticity](https://www.usmint.gov/american-eagle-2026-one-ounce-silver-proof-coin-26EA.html) from the Mint. The Mint has struck a proof almost every year since 1986, which makes a birth year or anniversary year easy to match. The exception is 2009. That year[no proof was struck at all](https://www.coinnews.net/2010/11/19/us-mint-2010-proof-silver-eagle-debuts/) , because silver blanks ran short and the law puts bullion Eagles first.


On Pure you will find proofs from the purple-box years of 1986 to 1992 through to recent dates, each listed with its box and certificate.


Be aware that a proof costs well over spot for its single ounce, because the finish and the packaging are most of what you are paying for. For the same reason, the box and certificate should stay with the coin for as long as the recipient owns it.


## 2. A bullion Silver Eagle in a capsule


This is the plain version of the coin above, and the cheaper way to give someone an ounce. By[federal law](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2023-title31/html/USCODE-2023-title31-subtitleIV-chap51-subchapII-sec5112.htm) it weighs 31.103 grams of .999 fine silver and measures 40.6 mm across. A bullion strike has no mintmark and a satin rather than mirrored finish, which is how you tell it apart from a proof.


It works for almost anyone, and best of all for a stacker whose tubes already hold Eagles.


## 3. A 10 oz silver bar


Ten troy ounces comes to about 311 grams, close to the weight of a can of soup. Pure carries older Engelhard pours alongside struck bars, sorted by series, and the[silver bars page](https://www.collectpure.com/marketplace/featured/silver-bars) has whatever is listed at the moment.


A troy ounce is heavier than the ounce on a kitchen scale, and[what a troy ounce is](https://www.collectpure.com/blog/what-is-a-troy-ounce) explains why.


## 4. A few silver rounds


Rounds look like coins but come from private mints, so they have no face value and aren't legal tender. With no face value and no collector finish, a round is priced mostly on its silver. A handful of them makes a modest gift that a stacker will actually use. The designs vary more than most people expect, and on Pure you will see 1 oz rounds carrying the Walking Liberty, Mercury dime and incuse Indian Head designs, as well as stackable 1 oz and 2 oz rounds.


Rounds with holiday designs are their own category, and[Christmas silver coins](https://www.collectpure.com/blog/christmas-silver-coins) covers those.


## 5. Junk silver by the dollar face


US dimes, quarters and halves dated 1964 and earlier are 90% silver. The[Coinage Act of 1965](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-79/pdf/STATUTE-79-Pg254.pdf) took silver out of the dime and quarter. Stackers call it junk silver and buy it by face value, not by the coin. The trade's working figure is[about 0.715 troy ounces of silver per $1 face](https://www.numismaticnews.net/us-coins/u-s-90-percent-silver-coins-best-silver-value) in circulated coins, allowing for wear.


Ten Mercury dimes in a small bag makes a good gift for someone who likes holding the metal. Pure sorts its 90% silver by type, so you can pick mixed dimes, Mercury or Barber dimes, or Standing Liberty quarters.[How to sell junk silver](https://www.collectpure.com/blog/how-to-sell-junk-silver) walks through the face-value math.


## 6. A silver Britannia


The Royal Mint's bullion coin is the right pick when their tubes are already full of Britannias. Since 2013 the silver Britannia has been .999 fine; before that it was .958, the older standard explained in[what Britannia silver is](https://www.collectpure.com/blog/what-is-britannia-silver) . The[2027 1 oz coin](https://www.royalmint.com/britannia/bullion/britannia-coins/britannia-2027-1oz-silver-bullion-coin/) is 38.61 mm across with a £2 face value and marks 30 years of the silver Britannia.


The[Britannia coins page](https://www.collectpure.com/marketplace/featured/britannia-coins) has the current listings.


## 7. A PAMP Lady Fortuna bar


Give this bar to someone who already owns plenty of plain ones. PAMP Suisse[introduced the Lady Fortuna design in 1979](https://www.pamp.com/our-brand/lady-fortuna) , the first artistic motif on its minted bars, and seals them in an assay card carrying an individual serial number. Among the listings on Pure is a 1 oz .999 silver Lady Fortuna bar struck for the design's 45th anniversary, still sealed in its card. Tell the recipient to leave that card sealed, since an unopened card is the only thing showing the bar inside is the one that was certified.


## 8. A scale that reads to 0.01 gram


A pocket scale with 0.01 g resolution costs little and checks a coin in seconds, and the target numbers are all published. A Silver Eagle should read 31.10 g, rounding from the 31.103 g the law sets, and a coin that reads well off that deserves a closer look from someone who tests metal. Weight alone cannot prove a coin is genuine, because a careful fake can match it, but it does catch the careless ones.


## 9. Tubes and capsules in the right size


Capsules and tubes are sized in millimeters, and the Eagle and the Britannia don't share a size: 40.6 mm against 38.61 mm. An Eagle will not fit a Britannia tube, and a Britannia rattles around in an Eagle tube, so buy tubes for whatever they actually stack. If their stack is mixed, capsules in both sizes are the safer choice.


## 10. A 5x to 7x loupe


[NGC recommends a 5- to 7-power triplet loupe](https://www.ngccoin.com/news/article/130/) for most coin work, along with a plain desk lamp, and advises against anything stronger. The same article files microscopes under expensive toys and warns that grading under heavy magnification almost always makes a coin look worse than it is.


## 11. A reference book on the coin they stack


For an Eagle stacker, the obvious one is[American Silver Eagles: A Guide to the U.S. Bullion Coin Program](https://whitman.com/american-silver-eagles-a-guide-to-the-u-s-bullion-coin-program-5th-edition-6x9) from Whitman. Its lead author, John Mercanti, was the Mint's chief engraver and[designed the heraldic eagle](https://coinweek.com/the-coin-analyst-john-mercantis-silver-eagle-guidebook/) on the coin's original reverse. The current edition is co-written with David Ryder, a former Director of the Mint, and goes through the series date by date.


## What to skip


Skip anything silver-plated, and skip novelty "silver" rounds that do not state a fineness. Circulating 2026 quarters belong here too, since they are copper-nickel clad like every circulating quarter since 1965, and while they make a nice stocking stuffer they are not silver. A stacker reads the fineness stamp before the design, and if there is no .999 or 90% on it, they will notice.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### Should I give a proof or a bullion Silver Eagle?


Go bullion if they stack for ounces, and proof if they have ever mentioned a year, a set or a box. Since a proof costs far more for the same ounce of silver, a stacker who does not collect proofs may well prefer two bullion coins to one proof.


### How do I know the silver is real?


Buy from somewhere that tests it. On Pure, every item is verified in house before it ships, items that pass ship Pure Qualified, and shipping is insured. The recipient can also put it on a scale, which is one more reason the scale above makes a good gift.


### What does "under spot" mean on a listing?


On Pure, sellers set their own asking prices against the live spot price, so some asks can sit below spot. The[silver under spot page](https://www.collectpure.com/marketplace/featured/silver-under-spot) shows listings priced below the spot price at the moment you view it, and it changes as spot moves and listings sell.[How buying under spot works](https://www.collectpure.com/blog/can-you-buy-silver-under-spot) explains why those asks exist.


### Can I have it shipped straight to them?


Set their address at checkout instead of changing it after the order is placed, and leave enough time before the date you need it.


## Where to start


If you know which coin they stack, buy them one more of it. If you do not, a bullion Silver Eagle is the easy default, and a 0.01 g scale is useful no matter what they stack. For a wider range across gold and silver,[gold and silver gift ideas](https://www.collectpure.com/blog/gold-and-silver-gift-ideas) covers the general list, and the[gold and silver gifts page](https://www.collectpure.com/marketplace/featured/gold-silver-gifts) shows giftable pieces listed on Pure today.
